Tim Cook reveals advice Steve Jobs gave him before handing over the reins as Apple CEO: 'Never ask what I would do'

Tim Cook recalled how Steve Jobs encouraged him to forge his own path rather than try to emulate his leadership style.

Updated on: Oct 20, 2026, 20:15:42 IST
By Bhavya Sukheja
Prefer HTon Google
Share via
Copy link
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:03
Instaread

Tim Cook recently revealed the one piece of advice Apple cofounder Steve Jobs gave him before handing over the reins as CEO of the tech giant: “Never ask what I would do, just do the right thing.”

Cook shared the advice in an interview with CBS Sunday Morning earlier this year, recalling how Jobs encouraged him to forge his own path rather than try to emulate his leadership style. “[Jobs’] advice to me was ‘Never ask what I would do, just do the right thing,’” Cook said in the interview.

The advice continues to influence Apple’s leadership nearly 15 years after Jobs died in October 2011. Cook, who joined Apple in 1998 and succeeded Jobs as CEO in 2011, said the cofounder wanted to ensure the company did not become paralysed by attempts to replicate his leadership style.

According to a report by Fortune, the advice stemmed from Steve Jobs’ observation of Disney. Notably, Jobs helped establish Pixar Animation Studios after purchasing the group from Lucasfilm in 1986. Disney later acquired Pixar in 2006, and during his work at the company, he noticed the company becoming paralysed by discussions about what its late founder Walt Disney would have done.

“He had watched Disney go through this paralysis of sitting around and talking about what Walt [Disney] would do. And he did not want that for Apple,” Tim Cook explained.

(Also Read: Tim Cook was happy at Compaq. One meeting with Steve Jobs changed his mind)

How Steve Jobs prepared Tim Cook for the CEO role

Tim Cook recalled that Apple had never experienced a “professional transition” at the CEO level, with earlier successions taking place during periods of crisis. Jobs wanted his departure from the top job to be different. So he invited Cook to his home and offered him the CEO position, while making it clear that his successor did not need to follow in his footsteps.

“I’ll never forget that and it was such a gift for me, because he took off of my shoulder this question of, ‘What would Steve do?’” Cook said. “I just put my head down and thought, ‘I’m going to be the best version of myself.’”

Cook joined Apple less than a year after Jobs returned to the company as interim CEO. He became chief operating officer (COO) in 2005 before taking over as CEO in 2011, following Jobs’ resignation due to his declining health.

Over nearly three decades at Apple, Cook said he learned which principles were central to the company’s identity. Those included collaboration, intense debate, focus and a commitment to excellence.

In the CBS interview, Cook described Jobs’ belief that collaboration could produce results greater than the sum of individual contributions.

“[Jobs] had the vision that the collaboration was something that would produce great results. That one plus one is equal to three, not two. That if you share an idea and debate it, it gets bigger and better,” Cook said. “If you care enough that you call somebody at 10 at night because you just had an idea, that incredible things can come out of that,” he added.

Cook also highlighted Jobs’ emphasis on prioritisation, saying the cofounder believed that meaningful progress required turning down countless ideas to focus on what mattered most.

“[Jobs] had an idea of focus that you say ‘no’ to a thousand things to say ‘yes’ to the one that’s truly important. And that when you do something, you should do it at an excellence level where good isn’t good enough: it has to be insanely great,” Cook said.

(Also Read: Apple-1 computer with Steve Wozniak's signature and rare letter from Steve Jobs sells for ₹10.9 crore at auction)

Steve Jobs’ advice to other business leaders

Tim Cook was not the only business leader to receive career-defining advice from Jobs. The Apple cofounder also influenced executives including Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz.

Benioff recalled on Lenny’s Podcast in 2024 that Jobs helped him overcome “entrepreneurs block”. Jobs challenged him to grow Salesforce’s business tenfold within two years, secure a major customer for its automation product and build an application economy.

Benioff interpreted the advice as a call to build an app store and went on to create AppExchange, Salesforce’s marketplace for business applications. He later gifted Apple the App Store trademark and the appstore.com domain, crediting Jobs’ guidance for its influence on his career.

Former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz also turned to Jobs for advice during a difficult period for the coffee chain in 2008. After Schultz discussed the company’s problems with him, Jobs recommended replacing the entire leadership team, arguing that the executives would eventually leave anyway. Schultz initially found the suggestion difficult to accept but later said Jobs had been right, as all but one member of the team eventually departed.

Apple-1 computer with Steve Wozniak's signature and rare letter from Steve Jobs sells for ₹10.9 crore at auction

The computer, known as the ‘Hatfield’ Apple-1, had a competitive 28-minute bidding battle between two people before fetching the record price.

Updated on: Oct 20, 2026, 18:45:11 IST
By Bhavya Sukheja
Prefer HTon Google
Share via
Copy link

An exceptionally rare, fully functional Apple-1 computer signed by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak recently sold at auction for $1.15 million (around ₹10.9 crore), setting a world record for a commercially released Apple-1.

According to a report by the New York Post, the computer, known as the ‘Hatfield’ Apple-1, had a competitive 28-minute bidding battle between two people before fetching the record price. The sale comes in the year Apple marks the 50th anniversary of its founding.

“We are delighted with this exceptional result for the ‘Hatfield’ Apple-1, one of the most important milestones in computing history,” Ian Ehling, a director at international auction house Bonhams, said, as per the Post. “It was an honor to offer Apple’s first product during the company’s 50th anniversary year,” he added.

The computer is particularly significant because its motherboard bears the clear signature of Wozniak, who designed and built the Apple-1 in 1976. Steve Jobs, on the other hand, was responsible for marketing the computer.

The auction lot also included a 1978 letter signed by Jobs and addressed to the computer’s original owner, Fred Hatfield. In the letter, Jobs offered Hatfield a trade-in upgrade to the newly released Apple II. Other items included in the sale were the original operations manual, a typed invitation to the “Apple I Owners Club” and several hardware components.

Harsh Goenka’s sharp take on Vinod Khosla’s chief of staff listing: ‘Available 24/7, sleep is a luxury’

Sun Microsystems co-founder and Khosla Ventures head Vinod Khosla posted that he is looking for a tech-savvy "thought partner" as his next chief of staff.

Updated on: Oct 21, 2026, 07:57:40 IST
By Trisha Sengupta
Prefer HTon Google
Share via
Copy link

Vinod Khosla’s recent chief of staff job opening, demanding 24/7 availability, long in-office hours in Menlo Park, and a multi-year commitment, drew a swift, satirical response from Harsh Goenka. In an X post, the RPG Group Chairman criticised the listing’s intense demands.

What are the requirements for the position?

Vinod Khosla, co-founder of Sun Microsystems and head of Khosla Ventures, posted last week that he is looking for his next chief of staff. The 71-year-old tweeted, “I'm hiring my next Chief of Staff. You won’t know every field I work in. What matters is how quickly you learn, the questions you ask, and whether you can think from first principles. You’ll help evaluate opportunities and work with founders building consequential companies. Technical background preferred. Three-year commitment. Menlo Park, in person.” He also shared a link to the job posting.

Also Read: Harsh Goenka highlights littering on Vande Bharat: ‘How to teach civic sense?’

The job requires the candidate to be a “thought partner to Vinod” while working with him directly. The responsibilities would include meeting with founders, assessing inbound opportunities, investigating technologies, writing investment recommendations and meeting briefs, tracking business performance, engaging with founders, and helping Khosla portfolio companies.

What, however, prompted a workplace debate was the requirements listed for the candidates. Among other things, the chief of staff is expected to “Work in person in Menlo Park every day, generally from 8 am to 8 pm,” as well as “Maintain around-the-clock availability, including nights and weekends when needed.”

Vinod Khosla hits back at critics:

Though the Silicon Valley venture capitalist is yet to respond to the Indian industrialist, Khosla - who has never shied away from hitting back at his critics - has responded to some tweets disagreeing with his job posting.

Also Read: Tinder CEO asked employees how they measured success, was met with blank stares

In one such post, he responded, “Jokes aside honest truth is this job has no specific hours requirement but is intense. I work 80 hours/week and this person needs to keep up. Doing, learning & more.... and very fun.”
